title: Can Your Team Still Coordinate When Your Systems Are Isolated?
summary: Regulators expect critical infrastructure operators to keep running when systems are isolated. Learn how your people coordinate. Register for the webinar.
body_markdown:
Since July 27, 2026,


[water and wastewater utilities in at least seven US states have reported intrusions into their control systems to the FBI](https://www.fbi.gov/investigate/cyber/alerts/2026/malicious-cyber-actors-targeting-water-and-wastewater-sector-internet--facing-programmable-logic-controllers-causing-operational-disruptions)


. Some saw degraded operations, including pressure loss and flooding. In Minnesota alone, more than 30 water systems were hit in one coordinated attack and some switched to manual operations.


In France this past October,


[a cyberattack on the refrigeration systems of hundreds of supermarkets](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/crq5nzxv9q4yo)


reportedly drove temperatures as high as 50°C (122°F), spoiling food and starting fires at several stores. The Paris prosecutor has opened an investigation.


In both cases, operators found out in real time whether their people could keep working when normal systems stopped behaving. Governments now want operators to make sure that critical systems can continue operating when operational technologies are isolated and offline.


## Regulators Now Expect Operators to Be Ready to Isolate and Keep Running


This July, Australia led the development of joint guidance called


[CI Fortify](https://www.blackberry.com/en/secure-communications/business/ci-fortify)


, issued with the US, UK, and Canada, telling critical infrastructure operators to be ready to isolate vital operational technology and keep running that way. The guidance is voluntary, but the mandates around it are not. The US, Canada, the UK, the EU, and Australia have each advanced cyber rules this year that change what operators must be able to do during a breach.


Read side by side, they make the same demands. Assume a breach and keep operating: plan for a compromise and keep essential services running through it. Put accountability above the IT team: in the EU, Australia, and Canada, responsibility reaches the board or directors. Prove a tested capability on the regulator's clock: every one of the five sets a reporting window.


## Why the Breakout Window Has Compressed to Minutes


[CrowdStrike's 2026 Global Threat Report](https://go.crowdstrike.com/2026-global-threat-report.html)


puts the average eCrime breakout time, from initial access to lateral movement, at 29 minutes in 2025, 65 percent faster than in 2024. The fastest observed breakout time took 27 seconds. The report also finds that AI-enabled adversaries increased their operations by 89 percent year over year, and says AI is accelerating attackers and compressing defenders' time to respond. At that speed, detect-and-evict is one layer of the response, not the whole plan.


## What Isolation Does to the People Running the Response


Isolation is a technical decision. What it does to your people is a separate problem, and most plans stop at the technical part.


When you isolate a network, the tools your people use to run the response often go down with it. Email carries field reports and status updates; when it goes, real-time field intelligence goes with it. Ticketing gives command one view of who is safe and what is being worked; when it goes, so does personnel visibility across the response. Directory and single sign-on are how outside agencies authenticate into your environment; when they go down, inter-agency sharing stops entirely, not because of a decision but because the access path is gone. Desk phones and softphones narrow your reach, but they are rarely the only casualty.


The org chart does not change during an incident. The tools your organization uses to run it can all disappear at once.


## What Your Team Must Be Able to Answer Before an Incident


Before an incident, your team should be able to answer:


1.


Could incident command reach your field staff?


2.


Could you verify who is on a call without your directory and single sign-on?


3.


Could you share information with an outside agency?


4.


Could you file your incident report inside the regulator's window?


If any answer is "not sure," that is the gap requiring attention.
